article.title: Jellyfin Loses Project Leader and Two Longtime Members in Nine Days as Burnout and an AI-Tooling Dispute Collide
article.summary: Jellyfin's project leader, a core team member, and a longtime contributor left within nine days, citing burnout and friction over AI-assisted development.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

Jellyfin, the open-source self-hosted media server, lost its project leader and two other longtime contributors within a nine-day span in July, in a leadership shake-up that its own departing leader described as amicable but that also surfaced an internal dispute over AI-assisted coding tools. According to [Linuxiac](https://linuxiac.com/jellyfin-loses-project-leader-and-core-team-member-in-major-shake-up/), project leader Joshua Boniface and longtime core team member Anthony Lavado left their roles effective July 19, 2026, only days after Andrew Rabert, described as one of the project's original figures, stepped away from the Jellyfin organization on July 17.

## What We Know

Boniface announced his and Lavado's departures in a post on [Jellyfin's official community forum](https://forum.jellyfin.org/t-project-leadership-changes), writing that "Anthony and I decided to depart from the project, myself as Project Leader, and he as a core team member. This is in addition to the resignation of Andrew on Friday." The change was also reflected in a GitHub pull request titled ["Remove Joshua Boniface and Anthony Lavado"](https://github.com/jellyfin/jellyfin.org/pull/1947), which was merged into the project's website repository.

Boniface, who has led Jellyfin since it launched in late 2018 as a fully open-source fork of Emby, according to [Linuxiac](https://linuxiac.com/jellyfin-loses-project-leader-and-core-team-member-in-major-shake-up/), cited burnout as his reason for stepping aside. "I simply could no longer provide the effort (mental or time-wise) that the role demanded, and thus I was not performing my duties to an acceptable degree, facing severe burnout, and risks to my mental health. It was time to step aside," he wrote on the forum. He added that the hand-off is "amicable" and that "there is good communication lines, so there is little to no risk of a hostile fork or anything of that nature." Reflecting on the project's growth, Boniface wrote: "Now here we are 7-and-a-half years later, and it's the #1 FLOSS media server, a truly viable alternative to Plex for literally millions of server administrators and probably 10x that many individual users."

Lavado, who according to Linuxiac managed app store operations, public outreach, releases, finances, and other administrative tasks rather than active coding, posted his own explanation on the same forum thread: "After 7.5 - nearly 8 - years, it's been a long time since I've been able to give much of my free time to Jellyfin. My life is changing and I've got other things that must take priority." He added that he is "fully committed to a smooth transition," even if it takes up to a year.

Rabert's departure followed a different path. In a [GitHub issue](https://github.com/andrewrabert/jellium-desktop/issues/609) posted July 17, he wrote that he had left "the Jellyfin organization entirely" after "burnout working within the Jellyfin organization." Rabert said he had started rewriting Jellyfin's desktop client in December 2025 to fix "long-standing problems in the previous desktop app (ie. HDR support, maintenance issues with Qt)," but that "only a handful of organization members" supported his approach, and that "the general attitude was very negative and increasingly burdensome and restrictive." He wrote that this "eventually reached a point where I lost almost all motivation to dedicate my time to this," calling the project "my passion - my default hobby to relax." His client has since been moved outside the official project and renamed Jellium Desktop, according to [Linuxiac](https://linuxiac.com/jellyfin-loses-project-leader-and-core-team-member-in-major-shake-up/); the [GitHub repository](https://github.com/andrewrabert/jellium-desktop) now describes it as "an unofficial desktop client for Jellyfin" and has drawn more than 1,500 stars.

Linuxiac reported that Rabert's exit followed "increasing disagreements over the development approach, including opposition to his use of AI-assisted tools." Rabert's own resignation post points to a specific flashpoint: he cited [an issue](https://github.com/andrewrabert/jellium-desktop/issues/109) filed against his client in April as "an early sign" of the friction. That issue, titled "Inclusion of CLAUDE.md violates Jellyfin LLM policy against inclusion of LLM metafiles," argued that a Claude Code configuration file in his repository broke [Jellyfin's official LLM policy](https://jellyfin.org/docs/general/contributing/llm-policies/), which states that contributors must "not commit LLM metafiles (e.g. .claude configs) or any other editor-created non-code files." That same policy document notes the project is "seeing a precipitous rise in contributors using AI within the Jellyfin ecosystem, both in the server and for clients, as well as a rise in criticism and concern about LLMs generally."

## What We Don't Know

Neither Boniface's nor Lavado's public statements named a successor as project leader, and Linuxiac reported that the close timing of the three departures "raises questions about Jellyfin's governance and who will take responsibility for the many duties previously handled by its longtime leaders." It is also not yet clear whether Rabert's AI-tooling dispute will affect how the remaining Jellyfin team treats other unofficial, AI-assisted client projects going forward.

## Why It Matters

Boniface and Lavado both framed the transition as low-risk, with Boniface writing that Jellyfin remains "in the very capable hands of the remaining team who have been driving the project for many years now," and Linuxiac found no indication that the server, its applications, or its repositories are being abandoned. But the departures still remove, within nine days, the person who started the project and two others who had been with it for roughly eight years, at a moment when the broader open-source world is still working out how contributors are allowed to use AI coding assistants.
